title: Binary Number with Alternating Bits
prompt: Given a positive integer `n`, check whether it has alternating bits, meaning no two adjacent bits in its binary representation have the same value. Return `true` if so, otherwise return `false`.

examples.explanation: The binary representation of 5 is 101, which alternates.
The binary representation of 7 is 111, which has adjacent equal bits.
The binary representation of 10 is 1010, which alternates.

hints: You could extract each bit and compare it with its neighbor one at a time.
Compare n with itself shifted right by one bit using XOR — alternating bits produce a very specific pattern.

If n's bits alternate, then (n XOR (n >> 1)) is a number consisting of all 1 bits (like 111...1). A number of all 1 bits, when incremented, becomes a power of two, so check if ((n ^ (n >> 1)) + 1) has exactly one set bit.

solution.approach: If n's bits alternate, XORing n with itself shifted right by one produces a number whose binary form is all 1s, because every adjacent pair of differing bits turns into a 1 at that position. A number made entirely of 1 bits, say of the form 2^k - 1, has the property that adding 1 to it yields exactly 2^k, a power of two with a single set bit. So compute m = n ^ (n >> 1), then check that m & (m + 1) == 0, which confirms m is all 1 bits.
